faq.title: What people ask before they enquire
faq.lead: Straight answers about how we work, what we weave, and how to start a commission or purchase.
faq.where_a: Every carpet is hand-knotted in our own workshops in Kathmandu, Nepal — on our looms, by our weavers. We do not outsource production.
faq.custom_q: Can you weave a custom size, colour, or design?
faq.custom_a: Yes. We take bespoke commissions — size cut to the centimetre, palette and motif developed with you, and fibre chosen for the room. Start on the custom orders page or contact us with dimensions and reference images.
faq.materials_a: Wool, silk, hemp, nettle, bamboo, linen, pashmina, and banana — alone or in blends. Each piece in the collection is tagged by the fibres it contains.
faq.order_q: How do I buy or enquire about a piece?
faq.order_a: There is no online checkout. Use the contact form, email, or WhatsApp to ask about availability, pricing, and shipping. Reference a design number from the collection page if you have one.
faq.visit_q: Can I visit the workshops in Kathmandu?
faq.visit_a: Yes. Many clients visit to walk the looms, meet weavers, and choose fibres and colours in person. Contact us to plan a visit alongside browsing the collection.
faq.ethics_q: What ethical standards do you follow?
faq.ethics_a: Our production is child-labour-free and aligned with GoodWeave standards. Carpets are hand-knotted in-house — not machine-made — and finished to export quality in Kathmandu.
faq.lead_q: How long does a custom commission take?
faq.lead_a: Lead time depends on size, knot count, and design complexity. We give an honest timeline when you enquire — typically weeks to months for larger pieces, not days.
faq.shipping_a: Yes. We export carpets worldwide. Shipping method, packing, and documentation are confirmed when you enquire — we handle export finishing in Kathmandu.

heritage.title: A craft that still lives in the hands
heritage.p1: At Kantipur, carpet weaving is folk art — a lineage of community, belief, and design carried by Nepalese weavers who still sit at the loom.
heritage.p2: Pieces are hand-knotted with the double-knot technique and a high pile density: slow work that locks colour into natural fibre and gives the surface its depth.
heritage.p3: We keep that practice close — not as a museum story, but as daily work: wool, silk, hemp, nettle, and the patience to finish something meant to outlast a season.

heritagePage.heroTitle: A craft that crossed the Himalaya and stayed
heritagePage.heroLead: From Tibetan looms in 1959 to two hundred workshops in the Kathmandu valley today — the story of how hand-knotted carpet became Nepal's living export, and how Kantipur kept it in human hands.
heritagePage.heroImageAlt: Weavers at vertical looms in a Nepali carpet workshop
heritagePage.introP1: At Kantipur, carpet weaving is folk art — a lineage of community, belief, and design carried by Nepalese weavers who still sit at the loom. Colour, religion, and pattern pass through generations; each piece is finished slowly so the fibre can hold light the way it was meant to.
heritagePage.introP2: We took our name from Kantipur — what Kathmandu was called first, from kānti, light, and pur, place. The city became a carpet capital within a decade of the first looms arriving. We build on that inheritance without treating it as nostalgia.
heritagePage.introP3: What you receive from us is not a commodity line — it is pile set knot by knot on vertical looms, in workshops we control, by adult weavers we can name.
heritagePage.introImageAlt: Hand-knotted samples and finished carpets in the Kantipur showroom
heritagePage.timelineEyebrow: How Kathmandu became a carpet city
heritagePage.timelineTitle: Five moments that shaped the craft here
heritagePage.t_1959_body: Tibetan families settle in the Kathmandu valley after 1959, bringing vertical looms and the rod-and-loop knot — a technique unlike the Persian or Turkish double knot used elsewhere in Asia.
heritagePage.t_1960_body: The refugee camp at Jawalakhel in Lalitpur becomes a weaving centre — giving the craft a workshop floor, a standard, and a path from household skill to livelihood.
heritagePage.t_1990s_body: Hand-knotted carpets become Nepal's largest export industry — at their peak, close to two-thirds of everything the country sold abroad. Kathmandu fills with looms, dyers, and buyers from Europe, Japan, and America.
heritagePage.t_2000s_body: Global scrutiny forces change: child-labour-free weaving, workshop transparency, and export certifications such as GoodWeave. Responsible makers rebuild trust — keeping production on their own floor so standards are verifiable.
heritagePage.t_today_body: Kantipur Carpet Craft Industries runs over two hundred looms, nearly twelve hundred adult Nepalese weavers, and more than five hundred designs — shipping from our own workshops to the Gulf, Asia, Europe, and the Americas.
heritagePage.knotTitle: Rod, loop, cut — the senna way
heritagePage.knotLead: Every Kantipur carpet is hand-knotted on a vertical loom using the Tibetan rod-and-loop method. It is not machine tufting, and it is not the Persian symmetric knot — which is why Himalayan pile feels different underfoot.
heritagePage.knotStep1Body: The weaver lays a gauge rod in front of the vertical warp threads. Its thickness sets the pile height — the foundation of every grade from 60 to 100 knots per square inch.
heritagePage.knotStep2Body: Yarn is wound around the rod and the warp in a single running loop — the senna loop. One motion, one node. The weaver moves along the row without breaking the yarn.
heritagePage.knotStep3Body: Loops are cut along the rod, leaving upright pile that wears evenly. The carpet grows row by row — a grid of knots that can take months on a large piece.
heritagePage.knotNote: Most of Asia ties a Persian or Turkish knot with two nodes per knot. Our rod-and-loop tradition is particular to the Himalayan line — double-knotted in density, singular in method.
heritagePage.knotImageAlt: Close detail of hand-knotted wool and silk pile
heritagePage.loomsTitle: Two hundred looms on our own floor
heritagePage.loomsLead: We maintain our own factories — not anonymous subcontracting — so quality, labour conditions, and delivery stay in our hands from the first sketch to the final roll.
heritagePage.loomsP1: Each loom is manned by weavers who learned the craft on the floor — taught by those who learned it the same way. A large commission can bind one person's attention for months, and it is finished by the same hands that started it.
heritagePage.loomsP2: Special orders from narrow runners to hall-sized carpets — hand-knotted, graded by knot count, and finished in our Kathmandu workshops before they leave for a buyer's room.
heritagePage.loomsImageAlt: Finished carpets rolled and stacked in the Kantipur warehouse
heritagePage.materialsTitle: Eight fibres, chosen for the design
heritagePage.materialsLead: Our catalogue spans wool, silk, hemp, nettle, bamboo, linen, pashmina, and banana — largely natural fibre, with vegetable-dyed and undyed options where the design calls for them.
heritagePage.fibre_wool: The workhorse — warm, resilient, and the backbone of most room-sized pieces.
heritagePage.fibre_silk: Fine detail and luminous colour — where 100 K.N. and curved motifs earn their keep.
heritagePage.fibre_hemp: Textural, earthy pile — often woven at 80 K.N. for contemporary and natural interiors.
heritagePage.fibre_nettle: A Himalayan fibre with a dry, matte character — prized for natural and undyed work.
heritagePage.fibre_bamboo: Light and smooth in blend — adds structure without weight in mixed-fibre designs.
heritagePage.fibre_linen: Cool clarity in wool-linen and silk-linen blends — for lighter, modern palettes.
heritagePage.fibre_pashmina: The finest handle — in pashmina-silk mixtures for pieces that ask to be touched.
heritagePage.fibre_banana: Unusual sheen and strength — a speciality fibre for distinctive texture.
heritagePage.peopleTitle: Every knot has a person behind it
heritagePage.peopleLead: Close to twelve hundred adult Nepalese weavers work our looms — the same figure our own published materials have carried for years. No piece is woven outside workshops we control.
heritagePage.peopleP1: Weaving is taught on the loom, not in a classroom. Skill stays in the valley because the work stays here — keeping the craft alive for another generation rather than outsourcing it away.
heritagePage.peopleP2: Since the industry reforms of the 1990s, responsible Nepalese makers weave child-labour-free. We keep production on our own floor so that standard is verifiable when a buyer asks.
heritagePage.peopleImageAlt: Weavers working at vertical looms in the Kantipur workshop
heritagePage.housesTitle: One workshop standard, two design voices
heritagePage.kantipurBody: K.C.C.I is the house behind this site — hand-knotted Nepalese rugs in natural fibres, from first sketch to final knot, with over five hundred designs and commissions shaped to the room you actually have.
heritagePage.changBody: C.C.M.I is our sister concern — specialised in contemporary American-leaning design, with vegetable dyes, loop-and-cut textures, wool-silk and pashmina-silk mixtures, and antique weaves recreated by the same Nepalese weavers.
heritagePage.pull: Carpet weaving is a folk art — generations, heritage, and the way we say what we believe.
heritagePage.ctaTitle: See where your carpet is made
heritagePage.ctaBody: Walk our workshops in Kathmandu, meet the weavers, and choose the piece — or commission — your project needs.

about.imageAlt: Detail of wool and silk hand-knotted carpet
about.p1: Kantipur Carpet Craft Industries (K.C.C.I) makes hand-knotted Nepalese rugs for rooms that want lasting beauty — natural fibres, our own workshops, and designs that touch the senses rather than shout from a catalogue.
about.p2: From first sketch to final knot, someone from the house stays with the piece. Our sister concern, Chang Carpet Manufacturers Industries (C.C.M.I), specialises in contemporary American-leaning design while keeping traditional charm and vegetable-dyed, loop-and-cut textures in play.
about.p3: Today more than two hundred looms and nearly twelve hundred adult Nepalese weavers work over five hundred designs — for intimate rooms and for commissions large enough to fill a hall.

custom.cap_colour_body: Vegetable dye, undyed natural tones, or a palette developed from your swatches and the light in the room.

soul.nameTitle: A carpet house, not a carpet factory
soul.nameBody: Kantipur Carpet Craft Industries keeps its own workshops in the Kathmandu valley, so quality and delivery never leave our hands. We took the name from Kantipur — what the city was called first, from kānti, light, and pur, place.
soul.imageAlt: Hand-knotted samples hanging above stacked carpets in the Kantipur showroom
soul.originP1: The technique we weave with arrived in this valley with Tibetan families after 1959. Within a decade a household craft had become a livelihood, and Kathmandu became a carpet city.
soul.originP2: We build on that inheritance and hold it to our own standard: the same upright looms, the same rod-and-loop knot, and the insistence that a Kantipur carpet should outlive the room it was bought for.
soul.timelineEyebrow: How the craft reached this workshop

soul.t_today_body: Kantipur runs over two hundred looms and five hundred designs, and ships them worldwide.
soul.pull: Carpet weaving is a folk art — generations, heritage, and the way we say what we believe.

knot.title: Knot count is resolution
knot.lead: A carpet is a grid. The tighter the knots, the finer the detail it can hold, and the longer it takes to weave. Everything we make is graded on this one axis.
knot.step1Body: The weaver lays a gauge rod in front of the vertical warp threads. Its thickness decides the pile height.
knot.step2Body: Yarn is wound around the rod and the warp in a single running loop — the senna loop, not a tied knot.
knot.step3Body: The loops are cut along the rod, leaving one node per loop — and a pile that stands upright and wears evenly.
knot.uniqueNote: This rod-and-loop method is particular to the Tibetan tradition. Most of Asia ties a Persian or Turkish knot instead, with two nodes to a knot — which is why a Himalayan pile feels different underfoot.
knot.macroAlt: Macro photograph of hand-knotted hemp and wool pile
knot.density60: 60 knots — a broad, textural weave. Flatweaves and loop pile, where the fibre itself is the pattern.
knot.density80: 80 knots — the workhorse grade. Enough definition for most designs, and the density most of our hemp and wool is woven at.
knot.density100: 100 knots — fine detail. Where silk blends earn their keep: curves hold, and small motifs stay readable.

house.title: Four decades of the same standard
house.lead: Kantipur Carpet Craft Industries runs its own workshops, so quality and delivery stay in our hands from the first sketch to the final knot. Our sister house, Chang Carpet Manufacturers Industries, carries the American designs.
house.marketsBody: Kantipur carpets leave our Kathmandu workshops for private clients, hotels and showrooms — from the Gulf and South Asia to Europe, North America and beyond. Each order is woven to the size, colour and certification it calls for, and shipped from our own floor.

people.title: Every knot has a person behind it
people.lead: Close to twelve hundred adult Nepalese weavers work our looms. A large piece can hold months of one person's attention, and it is finished by the same hands that started it.
people.imageAlt: Weavers at vertical looms in a Nepali carpet workshop
people.handsTitle: Made by hand, start to finish
people.handsBody: No machine sets the knots. The loom, the rod and the shears do the work, exactly as they did sixty years ago.
people.familyTitle: Adults only, on our own floor
people.familyBody: We keep our own workshops rather than subcontracting, so we can answer for who weaves each piece and under what conditions.
people.fairTitle: Skill that stays in the valley
people.fairBody: Weaving is taught on the loom, by people who learned it the same way. Keeping the work here is how the craft survives another generation.

standards.title: Ethically made, traceable to our floor
standards.lead: Nepal's carpet trade rebuilt itself around adult labour, workshop transparency and export-grade quality control. Kantipur holds to that same standard — not as marketing language, but as how the house actually runs.
standards.adultBody: Close to twelve hundred adult Nepalese weavers work our looms — the same figure our own published materials have carried for years. No piece is woven outside workshops we control.
standards.childFreeBody: Since the industry reforms of the 1990s, responsible Nepalese makers weave child-labour-free. We keep production on our own floor so that standard is verifiable, not assumed.
standards.handKnottedBody: Every carpet is hand-knotted on vertical looms — the Tibetan rod-and-loop technique, not machine tufting or power looms. What you receive is pile set knot by knot.
standards.naturalBody: Wool, silk, hemp, nettle and blends from our catalogue — largely natural fibre, with vegetable-dyed and undyed options where the design calls for them.
standards.traceableBody: We do not anonymous subcontracting. Quality, labour conditions and delivery stay in our hands from the first sketch to the final roll — Kantipur Carpet Craft Industries, Kathmandu.
standards.complianceBody: Buyers in Europe, the Gulf, Asia and North America often require GoodWeave licensing, quality audits, country-of-origin documentation or project-specific compliance. We weave to those specifications and supply certification on request.
standards.footnote: If your project requires a named standard — GoodWeave, buyer audit, or country-of-origin paperwork — tell us when you inquire and we will confirm what applies to the piece.
